newsitem.title: CANADA: Better Canadian trade balance seen spurring growth.
newsitem.headline: Better Canadian trade balance seen spurring growth.

text.p: Canada's balance of trade will continue to improve, adding significantly to Canada's overall near-term growth and padding its current account surplus, a report by a Canadian economic research institution said.

A C$30 billion (US$21.9 billion) improvement in the current account since 1993 has brought the balance into positive territory at about C$1.0 billion (US$732.4 million), said the Conference Board of Canada on Thursday.
Continued increases will lift this figure to above C$10 billion (US$7.32 billion) during the next two years, the report predicted.
"Our balance of trade just keeps improving," said Peter Hall, the board's senior research associate. "Canada's real trade balance now stands at its highest point in a decade."
Hall said net trade activity had added 0.7 percent annually to Canada's GDP since 1992.
Canada's export growth, however, will be lower than in recent years as North America experiences a slower, sustainable pace of economic expansion, the board said.
Overall, G7 economic growth will be constrained by ongoing fiscal restraint and weak consumer spending.
Collective G7 growth is forecast to reach 2.2 percent in 1997 and 2.3 percent in 1998, with inflation expanding at an average pace of 2.3 percent, the board said.
The Asia-Pacific bloc will remain the leader among regional economies, expanding by 3.3 percent in 1997 and 3.8 percent in 1998, the board said.

"Japan continues to be the weak link. North American expansion will continue along at an average rate of 2.4 percent during the next two years, while Western Europe will grow at a disappointing 2.3 percent in 1997," the board said.
